HeteroMosaic's split prefill, checked on our stack#

HeteroMosaic (UIUC + AMD, MICRO 2026, arXiv 2607.12839, UIUC-ChenLab/heteroMosaic, Apache-2.0) is the closest published work to a direction we already have: the XDNA 2 NPU and the Radeon iGPU working on one prompt at the same time. On our box (Ryzen AI MAX+ 395) they report prefill 1.17x over iGPU-only, decode neutral. This page is what of it transfers here, by measurement, and what we will not do.

Nothing of their tree is built or shipped. Their prebuilt NPU binaries (hw_bins/, npu2) are not used, their ROCm 7.1.1 / kernel 6.11 / AOCL stack is not installed on this box, and no code was copied: the harness below drives our kernels — ggml-hrx MUL_MAT for the iGPU and our own gemm_q4_prefill (IRON/mlir-aie) for the NPU — with their design as the hypothesis.

What their design is (read from the source, not the abstract)#

idea where what it means for us
M-split prefill GEMM hetero_compute.cpp:111 (..._gemm_packed_M), split at :191, disjoint row ranges into the same output, no join pass exploitable only if the two engines' throughputs are comparable
K-split for the down_proj shape hetero_compute.cpp:282, two pre-split weight buffers, join = output_2d.add_() at :444 same throughput condition, plus a padded reduction
Ratio is a calibration table, not a formula config_map (npuSetup.cpp:85), keyed (M,K,N,layer,chunk); seeded then swept by py/unified_llm_w4a16/_hetero_tune.py:97-118, :2208-2225 their tuned NPU share on Strix Halo is M/8 (strixP 1/2, krackanP 7/8) — i.e. they expect NPU:GPU ≈ 1:7
One packed W4A16 layout for both engines 4352-byte tile = 4096 B nibble-packed 128×64 weights + 128 B bf16 scales + 128 B zeros (hipkernels/w4a16_gemm_packed.cu:35-39), packer py/.../qwen25_14b_w4a16_model.py:662-793 the single best idea in the paper for us: one weight copy in DRAM, consumed by HIP and by the NPU
DRM shareable buffers HIP allocates and exports (hsa_amd_portable_export_dmabuf), amdxdna imports (PRIME_FD_TO_HANDLE) — npuSetup.cpp:1913-2010, handles in bo_args[4] at :1836 we can do this too, and we already have the export hook: ggml_backend_buffer_export_dmabuf (ggml-hrx.cpp:1125)
Chunked prefill + host dispatcher per-chunk HIP streams (unified_llm_w4a16.cpp:2179-2260), NPU work in std::async threads gated by a 16-event pool (hetero_compute.cpp:36-41) spinning on hipEventQuery (npuSetup.cpp:1852-1872) the "scheduler" is a mutex (npu_mutex, npuSetup.cpp:1827) plus hand-tuned stage_bubbles delays in the config; there is no coalescing thread in the code

Two things the paper's summary gets wrong about the code, worth having straight because they change what we would port: requests are not coalesced at run time (one global mutex serialises the array; only PDI/instruction contexts are shared), and cross-engine ordering is host-side polling of a HIP event, because amdxdna has no wait-on-HIP-fence. The NPU submission also rebuilds two command BOs per GEMM call (npu_matmul_func.cpp:325-430).

What we measured#

Harness ~/mosaic-bench/mosaic_bench (ours): one process, the engine's ggml-hrx MUL_MAT on HRX0 for the iGPU and our gemm_q4_prefill NPU kernel through XRT (T=256 rows/launch), each alone and then both concurrently with rows split. Shapes are Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-4B prefill GEMMs, M = 256 / 2048 / 16384 prompt tokens. Every run under npu-hold outside gpu-hold, one ticket at a time. The NPU side was validated against the kernel's own fp64 fixture first (rel_fro=2.22e-3, their gate 5e-3), so the timings are of a correct kernel.

iGPU alone (HRX, Q4_K weights, ms / TFLOP-s):

shape model M=256 M=2048 M=16384
up_gate 2560×9728 4B 0.383 / 29.1 2.80 / 36.4 20.03 / 40.7
down 9728×2560 4B 0.489 / 26.1 3.38 / 29.5 21.21 / 38.5
up_gate 1024×3072 0.6B 0.455 / 3.5 0.60 / 21.2 8.58 / 11.9
down 3072×1024 0.6B 0.274 / 5.9 0.67 / 19.3 4.03 / 25.6

Independent anchor, not my microbench: llama-bench -p 2048 -n 0 --device HRX0 on Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M = 1372.8 tok/s, i.e. 11.0 TFLOP/s for the whole prefill with attention and dequant included. The single-op numbers above are upper bounds; the anchor is what a split would actually compete with.

NPU alone (our gemm_q4_prefill, T=256): per-tile time is flat in M — 8.61-8.66 ms for the 4B shapes, 1.15-1.30 ms for the 0.6B shapes — so 1.47-1.58 TFLOP/s (4B) and 1.24-1.40 TFLOP/s (0.6B), and total NPU time is ceil(M/256) × tile. It is weight-stream bound: the design refetches the whole weight column for every T-tile, which is why the per-tile time tracks K·N and not T.

Together (M-split, wall clock, best ratio per shape):

shape M iGPU alone best split speed-up
4B up_gate 16384 20.03 ms m=15872, NPU 2 tiles 1.013x
4B down 16384 21.21 ms m=15872, NPU 2 tiles 1.001x
0.6B up_gate 16384 8.58 ms m=15872, NPU 2 tiles 1.009x
4B up_gate 2048 2.85 ms m=1792, NPU 1 tile 0.32x
4B down 2048 3.38 ms m=1792, NPU 1 tile 0.41x
0.6B down 2048 0.67 ms m=1792, NPU 1 tile 0.53x
any measured shape 256 0.16-0.49 ms — ≤ 0.37x

The result: on this box the M-split never wins. It is +1.3 % at best, in the one regime where the NPU's share fits entirely under the iGPU's (2 tiles = 17.2 ms under 19.4 ms of GPU work), and any larger NPU share loses 2-12x. It is not interference — with the NPU busy the iGPU's own time does not move (a 16384-row GEMM costs 20.03 ms alone, and the whole split took 20.06 ms while the NPU streamed 8.6 ms alongside; the NPU's 1.8 GB/s of weights is 1 % of DRAM bandwidth, and this matches the GPU-busy NPU measurement in Hybrid, which keeps 87 % of NPU bandwidth in the other direction). It is plain throughput asymmetry: our iGPU runs these GEMMs at 29-41 TFLOP/s and our NPU at 1.5 TFLOP/s, a 20-25x ratio, so the ceiling on any split is ~3-5 % and only at M=16384.

Their 1.17x is therefore not contradicted, it is out of reach for a different reason: their own tuned NPU share (M/8 on this SoC) implies an NPU:GPU ratio near 1:7 in their stack, and their iGPU path is a rocWMMA W4A16 kernel, not hipBLASLt-class throughput. Our GPU side is the fast half; there is nothing for the NPU to take that the GPU is slow at.

Re-measured after the 2026-11-01 11:13 GPU reset: the sentence above is conditional on the iGPU's state#

The table and the "never wins" verdict were measured on one boot (06:00-06:40 AST, before the reset). On the boot that followed the reset, the same harness, the same NPU kernel sets and the same shapes give a different iGPU:

shape M iGPU, pre-reset boot iGPU, post-reset boot
4B up_gate 2560×9728 2048 2.80 ms / 36.4 TFLOP-s 2.88 ms / 35.4 TFLOP-s
16384 20.03 ms / 40.7 TFLOP-s 65.68 ms / 12.4 TFLOP-s
4B down 9728×2560 16384 21.21 ms / 38.5 67.51 ms / 12.1
0.6B up_gate 1024×3072 16384 8.58 ms / 11.9 12.39 ms / 8.3
0.6B down 3072×1024 16384 4.03 ms / 25.6 9.71 ms / 10.6

M ≤ 2048 reproduces within 3 %, and a fresh-process M-sweep puts a hard knee between M=2048 (36.9 TFLOP-s) and M=4096 (12.5 TFLOP-s), linear above it.

The knee is a dispatch rule, not an accident: the Q4_K prefill path (common.mul_mat.q4_k_q8_1_x4_prefill) is capped at 256-2048 tokens, and Q4_K cannot use the split-tail relaxation because its head binds the weight in the packed Row64 layout, so every M above 2048 rides hip.dense_prefill.mm instead. That alone is not a problem — on the rc-2026-10-31c binaries the same GEMM at M=16384 runs at 18.6 ms / 43.95 TFLOP-s on this very boot, i.e. slightly better than the pre-reset numbers. The 12.4 TFLOP-s in the table above is what current main does with that kernel.

That gap is a build regression, isolated by crossing the two libraries: today's libggml-hrx is slow even when driving the older libhrx/libloomc, and the older libggml-hrx is fast even when driving today's, with the same dispatch and the same kernel corpus (335 code objects) in all four arms. Both sides are on llama.cpp pin 4a58da9b0, so it is build configuration rather than source. Filed as engine#782; clocks (2895 MHz, 72-78 C) and the box's GTT occupancy were ruled out, several builds each.

The consequence for the split is in the next table, and the honest reading of it is that a split's ceiling follows whatever the iGPU is currently doing — which, on main today, is 3.5x below what the same hardware does on the release candidate.

At that 8:1 iGPU:NPU ratio the split does win, and at the balance point rather than at M-256:

shape M iGPU alone best split speed-up
4B up_gate 16384 65.71 ms m=14848, NPU 6 tiles 1.098x
4B down 16384 67.66 ms m=14592, NPU 7 tiles 1.111x
0.6B up_gate 16384 12.73 ms m=14592, NPU 7 tiles 1.128x

One formula covers both boots: balance the iGPU's per-row time against the NPU's per-256-row-tile time. At 40.7 TFLOP-s that puts the optimum at m≈15800 and a 1.036x ceiling (what the earlier sweep saw as 1.013x at m=15872); at 12.1 TFLOP-s it puts it at m≈14600 and 1.10-1.13x (measured 1.098-1.128x). Overlap is effectively free either way: at the optimum the wall clock is within 0.5 % of the iGPU's own share of the rows, and amdxdna logged no errors across the runs.

Read together, the numbers say the split is a ratio question, not an NPU-quality question, and that the ratio is not a property of this SoC alone. They also say the split is not a mitigation: 59.8 ms of split on the degraded boot is still 3x slower than 20.0 ms of iGPU-only on the healthy one. A 10 % win taken from a 3.3x loss is not a reason to build a split dispatcher; it is a reason to keep the iGPU numbers of this document dated, and to re-run the ratio before anyone quotes a ceiling from it.

What transfers, and what we will not do#

Transfers (worth doing regardless of the split):

  • One packed weight layout both engines read. This is the idea with real value here, and it is also the answer to the hybrid route's biggest waste — the model resident twice (docs/hybrid.md, ~/briefs/TZEROCOPY-STATE.md row 12: a 15 GB GGUF plus a 16 GB model.q4nx). Their tile is a flat uint8 buffer with the scales and zeros inline, so a HIP kernel and an NPU instruction stream can both consume the same bytes with no repack. Ours are two packings today (ggml Q4_K blocks for HRX, Q4NX tiles for the NPU kernels).
  • The DRM buffer bridge. Measured, works, and we already own half of it (next section).
  • The dispatcher shape — one HIP stream per in-flight chunk, NPU work on its own thread, ordering by a recorded event — is what our hybrid route would need anyway, and it does not need their code.

Will not do:

  • Port their NPU binaries or their stack. Prebuilt .pdi/instruction blobs are theirs to ship, not ours to run; our NPU route is our own full-ELF kernel sets (docs/npu.md). Their ROCm 7.1.1 / kernel 6.11 / AOCL pins are not this box's.
  • Build a split-prefill dispatcher before the NPU GEMM is faster. A dispatcher around a 1.5 TFLOP/s NPU buys ≤ 1.3 %, measured. The precondition is an NPU prefill GEMM ~4x faster: our per-tile time is weight-fetch bound, so a T>256 tile with weight reuse across T is the work (roughly 4x at T=1024), and only then does a ~15 % split at M=16384 become possible — still 0 at M≤2048.
  • Copy the weights to give the NPU its own layout per layer. Measured cost: 50 MiB of copies per layer for the 4B up_gate (~3.6 ms at 14 GB/s) against a 1.3 % best-case gain.

The DRM buffer, measured#

~/mosaic-bench/dmabuf_test.cpp, 64 MiB, under npu-hold + gpu-hold:

step result
HRX allocation → ggml_backend_buffer_export_dmabuf → dma-buf fd fd in 0.044 ms
amdxdna PRIME_FD_TO_HANDLE + GET_BO_INFO + mmap 0.206 ms (0.090 ms for a plain hipMalloc)
iGPU writes → the amdxdna mapping reads, and the reverse MATCH both ways over 64 MiB, one buffer
bandwidth through the shared mapping 29.3 GB/s CPU read, vs 14.0 GB/s for hipMemset + hipMemcpy D2H
NPU-allocated BO → dma-buf (xrt::bo::export_buffer() + PRIME_HANDLE_TO_FD) fails (XRT's own handle, ENOENT) — only iGPU-allocated buffers are shareable

So the sharing half of their design is available to us today with our own export hook, and it is 2x the copy path. What is missing is execution on the imported buffer: our NPU kernels go through XRT, which allocates its own BOs and cannot bind a foreign dma-buf handle as a kernel argument. HeteroMosaic executes on imported handles only because it submits to amdxdna by raw ioctl (npuSetup.cpp:1913-2010), with no XRT in the path at all.

Follow-ups filed#

  • #753 — dma-buf import for the NPU submission path: XRT cannot bind an imported BO, so today only iGPU→NPU sharing is possible, and only for buffers the NPU cannot yet execute on.
  • #754 — split-prefill in the hybrid route, blocked on an NPU prefill GEMM with T>256 weight reuse; the numbers above are the acceptance bar it has to clear.
  • docs/hybrid.md's "Running beside the GPU" section already covers the other direction (an NPU stream under a busy GPU keeps 87 % of its bandwidth); this page adds the GPU-side view: the iGPU loses < 0.2 % when the NPU runs beside it.

Reproducing#

~/mosaic-bench/mosaic-run env ITERS=3 ./sweep.sh        # alone: HRX, NPU, first split sweep
~/mosaic-bench/mosaic-run env ITERS=3 ./sweep2.sh       # split at the ratios that matter
~/mosaic-bench/mosaic-run ./dmabuf_test --mode hip      # DRM bridge, HIP allocation
~/mosaic-bench/mosaic-run ./dmabuf_test --mode hrx      # DRM bridge, HRX allocation (engine hook)

mosaic-run sets what HRX needs on this box and takes the holds (HOLDS=gpu|npu|both). On the rebuilt box the 2026-10-01 ~/.local/share/1bit-canonical install cannot enumerate HRX0 at all (hrx_gpu_initialize → NOT_FOUND); the rc31c libraries plus the TheRock libhsa-runtime64.so.1 path can, and that is what the numbers above used.

Unrun, declared: Qwen3-4B q_proj (4096×2560) and 0.6B k/v (1024×1024) — our prebuilt kernel set has no such shapes and the mlir-aie venvs that would build them are gone on this box (~/ironenv142 empty, ~/iron → a dangling link). k/v/o/x-projection shapes we did measure are the two biggest per model (up/gate and down = 75 % of Qwen3-4B projection FLOPs). Also unrun: K-split (the down_proj K-split path), decode (the paper reports it neutral; our NPU serves decode through a different kernel), and anything end-to-end through serve.

Source of the analysis: ~/amd-oss/heteroMosaic at 61714a3, read-only, no build.
